meta.title: Cantonese A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Cantonese → English (see the Cantonese, recall the meaning) and English → Cantonese (see an English meaning, recall the Cantonese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. THIS IS SPOKEN HONG KONG CANTONESE, the language people talk in, not the written Chinese Hong Kong reads and writes, which is close to Mandarin: 佢 for he or she, 喺 for at, 嘢 for a thing, 睇 to look, and the sentence-final particles that carry a Cantonese speaker's tone of voice. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no examination publishes a graded word list for Cantonese, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 451 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — relatives and the people around you, jobs, work and school, clothes and shopping with an Octopus card, cooking, dim sum and cha chaan teng food, the furniture and chores of a flat, the town and its buildings, travel and directions by MTR, ferry and tram, the countryside, nature and animals, the seasons and typhoons, health and the body, feelings and character, free time, sport and the festivals (Lunar New Year and its red packets, Mid-Autumn and its mooncakes), more classifiers, telling what happened and when, comparing and giving an opinion, and the everyday verbs of moving, dressing and doing — and the other 299 are the commonest remaining words of spoken Cantonese, counted in the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus (recorded conversations and radio, 1997–98). The cards are dealt by how often the words are heard there and in Tatoeba's Cantonese sentences, so the commonest come first. Every headword is printed in the traditional characters Hong Kong uses, with the simplified form beneath where it differs, and in Jyutping, the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong's romanisation, which ends every syllable with its TONE as a digit: 1 high, 2 high rising, 3 mid, 4 low falling, 5 low rising, 6 low — because a Cantonese syllable said on the wrong tone is a different word (si1 poem, si4 time, si6 yes). The Cantonese Jyutping and Tones deck, the first in this collection, teaches the sounds and the six tones. The part of speech is the one the corpus's annotators gave the word, and the classifiers a noun is counted with are taught as words of their own rather than printed on the noun. Example sentences come with 410 of the 750 words, three apiece for 217 of them — Tatoeba's Cantonese is small, so many words have none — with the word picked out in colour, a speaker beside each sentence, and the Jyutping beneath it where every word in the sentence carries a reading the dictionaries confirm. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings: CC-CEDICT (MDBG, CC BY-SA 4.0) and CC-Canto (Pleco, CC BY-SA 3.0). Jyutping: CC-Canto and its Cantonese readings of CC-CEDICT (Pleco, CC BY-SA 3.0), and the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus. Frequency and parts of speech: the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus, HKCanCor (Luke Kang Kwong; CC BY 4.0, as distributed with PyCantonese), and Tatoeba. Example sentences and their Jyutping: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
